opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way the term has been used, at least in the work that sparked a lot of this conversation, is that an ability is "emergent" if it's absent in smaller models and then appears, often fairly sharply, in larger ones. You plot some task performance against model scale, and for a long stretch it's near zero, and then suddenly it jumps. And that's what got people excited, because it suggests unpredictability. You can't extrapolate from small models to know what a big model will be able to do.

What we wanted to do in our work was ask a slightly more careful question: is that sharpness a property of the model, or is it a property of how we're measuring the model? And what we found is that a lot of it comes down to the choice of metric. Many of the tasks where people reported emergence use metrics that are discontinuous or very harsh, things like exact string match or multiple-choice accuracy, where you get no credit unless everything is exactly right. If a model's per-token error rate is improving smoothly with scale, an all-or-nothing metric over a long sequence can turn that smooth improvement into something that looks like a sudden jump.

So when we took the same model outputs and scored them with continuous metrics, like token edit distance or the probability assigned to the correct answer, the curves mostly became smooth and predictable. We also showed you can go the other way: take vision models, where nobody had claimed emergence, and by choosing harsh metrics you can manufacture what looks like emergent behavior.

So my view on defining it is this. I'd separate two things. One is that capabilities appear at scale, which is obviously true. Bigger models do things smaller models can't do usefully. The other is the stronger claim that those capabilities show up sharply and unpredictably, and that's the claim I think we should be much more skeptical of. If you want to call something emergent in that strong sense, you should show that the transition holds up across reasonable metrics, ideally with enough evaluation data and enough model sizes that you're not just seeing sampling noise or sparse coverage of scale.

I don't say that to rule out real emergence. There may well be genuine phase-transition-like behavior in some settings. But the burden of proof should sit with the measurement, and practically this matters a lot. If capabilities are mostly predictable under the right metrics, that's good news for forecasting and for safety, because it means we can anticipate what's coming instead of being surprised by it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a weaker claim that capabilities appear at scale from a stronger claim of sharp, unpredictable onset, but does not identify technical and colloquial meanings as a source of ambiguity.

r002.rationale: It describes abilities that are absent in smaller models and appear in larger ones, often sharply, and says this suggests unpredictability that cannot be extrapolated from small models.

r003.rationale: It characterizes the reported pattern as task performance staying near zero and then suddenly jumping as model scale increases.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way the term has typically been used, going back to the paper from Jason Wei and colleagues, is that an emergent ability is one that's not present in smaller models but shows up in larger ones. And the key qualifier that made it interesting to people was that it seemed to appear sharply and unpredictably. You'd look at a plot of performance against scale, and it would be flat, flat, flat, and then suddenly jump. That's what gave it that almost mystical flavor, the idea that you can't anticipate what a model will do until you train it.

In our work, we tried to be a bit more careful about what that definition actually requires. We broke it into two properties. One is sharpness, meaning the transition from not having the ability to having it is discontinuous rather than smooth. The other is unpredictability, meaning you couldn't have extrapolated from the smaller models to see it coming. And what we found is that both of those properties are often artifacts of how you measure things rather than properties of the model itself.

The simplest example is accuracy on a multi-step task. If you're using exact match, a model has to get every token right to get credit. Per-token performance might be improving perfectly smoothly with scale, but when you compound that across a long sequence, you get something that looks like zero for a long time and then shoots up. Swap in a metric that gives partial credit, like token-level edit distance or log likelihood of the correct answer, and the curve becomes smooth and predictable. Nothing about the model changed. What changed is the lens.

So my view is that "emergence" as it's commonly used is really a statement about the relationship between a model, a metric, and the resolution of your measurements, not just about the model. That doesn't mean nothing interesting happens with scale. Capabilities clearly do improve. But the claim that we fundamentally can't forecast them deserves a lot more skepticism than it got, and I think that matters for how we talk about safety and planning around these systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the term’s typical use and its “mystical flavor,” but does not identify movement between technical and colloquial meanings as a source of ambiguity.

r002.rationale: It describes the ability as appearing in larger models but not smaller ones, and calls its onset unpredictable.

r003.rationale: It describes performance as flat across smaller models and then suddenly jumping as scale increases.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish two things. One is an ability that we didn’t anticipate. You train a model, you try something new, and it turns out to do surprisingly well. That’s a perfectly reasonable informal use of emergence.

The more specific claim is that an ability appears abruptly as you scale—that smaller models can’t do something, and then, beyond some size, larger models suddenly can. To evaluate that claim, you have to be careful about how you measure the ability.

Suppose you score a task as correct only if the model gets an entire sequence right. The model might be improving gradually on each part of that sequence, but your score makes that improvement look like a sudden jump. If you measure partial progress, you might see a much smoother curve.

So I’d define emergence operationally: What’s the task, what’s the metric, and what changes as we scale? The surprising capability can be real, while the apparent discontinuity is a consequence of how we chose to measure it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes an informal use of emergence from a specific scaling claim, but does not identify movement between technical and colloquial meanings as the source of ambiguity.

r002.rationale: It describes an unanticipated ability and separately discusses abrupt scaling, but does not characterize the onset of abilities as unpredictable as model scale increases.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes an ability appearing abruptly as models scale, with smaller models unable to do it and larger models suddenly able to.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to distinguish between an ability emerging and our measurement of that ability changing. Typically, people say an ability is emergent if you don’t see it in smaller models, and then, as you increase scale, it seems to appear quite suddenly.

But that apparent jump can depend quite a lot on how you measure performance. If your metric only gives credit for an exactly correct answer, you might see zero performance for a long time and then a sharp increase. If you instead measure how much probability the model assigns to the correct answer, you might see a much more gradual improvement.

So I’d want a definition that makes clear what ability we’re talking about, what measure we’re using, and what we mean by unexpected. A sudden change in a benchmark score is interesting, but by itself it doesn’t establish that the underlying capability appeared suddenly. That distinction matters if we want to understand—and eventually predict—what happens as these models get larger.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes an underlying ability from how it is measured, but does not identify movement between technical and colloquial meanings as a source of ambiguity.

r002.rationale: It asks what “unexpected” means and says prediction matters, but does not characterize the onset of abilities as unpredictable as scale increases.

r003.rationale: It describes an ability seeming to appear suddenly as models scale and gives the example of a sharp increase in exact-answer performance.
